name: Medial canthus theory

card.summary: A framework that treats the shape and height of the inner eye corner as part of what makes the eye area look sharp, opened or tired, and that guides which eye-area tweaks people consider.
card.note: Do-it-yourself cutting of the inner eye corner is discussed in forums but is surgery near the eye; clinicians perform canthal procedures under sterile conditions.

quick.overview:
The medial canthus is the inner corner of the eye, where the upper and lower lids meet next to the nose. In looksmaxxing discussion, its shape, depth and height relative to the outer corner are treated as one of the details that shape how the eye area reads, for example more almond and open versus rounder or more tired-looking.

The theory is mostly a way of analysing photos and choosing what to change. Anatomy references describe the region and the surgical literature covers canthal reconstruction, but no published study tests the looksmaxxing claims about inner-corner shape and attractiveness.
quick.how: In practice people compare their inner and outer eye corners in photos, then discuss options ranging from makeup and eyeliner placement to lash and eyebrow styling, cosmetic tattooing of the inner corner for a shading illusion, and surgical canthoplasty or canthopexy performed by oculoplastic or plastic surgeons. Results discussed are per individual photo comparisons.
quick.risks: Procedures on the eyelid corner carry the risks of eyelid surgery generally, including infection, scarring, asymmetry and tear-drainage problems, and the area sits close to the tear duct. Forum members themselves warn against self-cutting, and clinicians describe canthal work as a specialist procedure. The tattoo approach is discussed as subtle and has no published trial.

lead: The medial canthus is the inner corner of the eye, where the upper and lower eyelids meet toward the nose; anatomy sources describe a small triangular space there called the lacus lacrimalis and note that in some people the corner is partly covered by an epicanthic fold [1]. In looksmaxxing communities, "medial canthus theory" is the idea that the shape, depth and visible height of this corner, and its relationship to the outer corner, contribute to how striking, open or tired the eye area looks.

People who use the framework apply it to analysing their own photos and deciding which eye-area changes to explore. Options discussed include makeup and lash styling, a cosmetic tattoo at the inner corner meant to shade it and create an illusion of a lower inner and higher outer corner [2], and surgical procedures. One looksmax.org thread title announces "medial canthus and PFL lengthening surgeries" as newly available [3].

The theory sits next to better-known eye-area vocabulary such as canthal tilt, the angle between the inner and outer corners. Facial plastic surgeons quoted in beauty media describe a positive tilt (outer corner higher) as widely seen as attractive, while saying it is one feature among many and that overall facial balance matters more [11]. Published literature on the medial canthus itself covers anatomy and reconstruction in a medical context, such as tumour resection, lower-eyelid ageing and canthopexy [4][8][9][10]. No study located tests whether inner-corner shape changes perceived attractiveness.

chain: Analyse inner-corner shape and height against the outer corner
Choose a tweak (makeup, lash styling, cosmetic tattoo, or surgery by a specialist)
Eye area reads more open or defined in photos
angle.text: The theory gives people a vocabulary for what to adjust around the eye. Users describe makeup and subtle shading as the lower-commitment route and surgical canthoplasty or canthopexy as the clinical one. Appearance effects are reported from individual before and after photos.

paras: The canthus is either corner of the eye. The medial (inner) commissure extends a short distance toward the nose, and the lateral (outer) corner is sharper with the lids close to the globe. In cephalometric analysis the inner and outer corner points are called the endocanthion and exocanthion [1].

Related anatomical variation includes the epicanthic fold, which partly covers the inner corner in many East Asian and some Southeast Asian people, and telecanthus, where the inner corners sit farther apart, widening the look of the nasal bridge [1]. Reviews of lower-eyelid anatomy describe how the skin, muscle, tarsal plate and the ligament sling at the corners together determine eyelid position and appearance, and how ageing alters these layers [4].

The palpebral fissure is the elliptical opening between the two eyelids, bounded by the medial and lateral canthi; in adults it measures roughly 10 mm tall by 30 mm wide [12]. Clinicians describe a fissure as upslanted or downslanted, and certain genetic conditions are associated with characteristic slants [12]. Looksmaxxing uses the related term canthal tilt for the angle between inner and outer corners.

The epicanthic fold is a vertical skin fold beside the nose that can cover the inner corner. It is most common in East and Southeast Asian populations and in several other groups, and the same article notes it is nearly universal among adults in Japan and South Korea. It is also seen in many young children [13]. Because the fold hides the inner corner, discussion of inner-corner shape in forums often overlaps with the fold, and the surgical modification of folds is called epicanthoplasty [13][14].

Surgeons describe epicanthoplasty as technically demanding because the folds overlie the tear-drainage canals, and visible scarring is the main documented complication; a Z-shaped incision technique is described for scar correction [14]. Canthoplasty more broadly is defined as surgery on the medial and/or lateral canthus, used both cosmetically and for eyelid malposition [15].

Threads on looksmax.org ask how to get a "better medial canthus", whether to cut it for a more striking eye area, and whether such discussion is overblown [2][5][6]. One poster describes a TikTok creator who reported using outer lash lifting and inner-corner tattooing to counter drooping outer corners, aiming for a higher outer corner and lower inner corner in appearance; the poster found the after photo preferable while noting the angle and expression differed and another reply questioned whether filler was involved [2].

Other threads include strongly worded opposition to self-cutting, citing infection, pain and scarring beside the eye [5][7]. The community therefore holds both interest in the theory and open scepticism about the more invasive methods.

Beauty-press coverage of the canthal tilt trend describes a positive tilt, a neutral tilt and a negative tilt in which the inner corner sits higher [11]. New York facial plastic surgeon Edward Kwak is quoted saying tilt is not a primary factor when he evaluates eyes and advising against making surgical decisions on the basis of trends or filters; his colleague Konstantin Vasyukevich reports growing numbers of patients asking to lift the outer corner, and says attractiveness depends on overall facial balance [11].

The same coverage lists non-canthal options clinicians use for a tired or downturned look, including neurotoxins, fillers, blepharoplasty, brow lift and lid-shortening when lower-lid laxity is the cause [11]. This is the clinical counterpart to the tattoo-and-lash approach described by forum users.

Clinical literature describes canthal procedures in medical settings: periorbital reconstruction after tumour removal includes medial canthus repair [8][9], and a French-language report describes a transnasal canthopexy technique [10]. These are reconstructive or corrective operations by trained surgeons; they are distinct from the cosmetic goals described in forums.

No studies found that test medial canthus shape as a factor in attractiveness or that evaluate cosmetic canthus tattooing. Related clinical literature is reconstructive: a Tunisian series of 123 patients with eyelid cancers reported medial canthus reconstruction in 18 lesions [8], and reviews describe periorbital flap reconstruction [9].

timeline.event: A review in the Journal of Dermatologic Surgery and Oncology covers periorbital reconstruction including the medial canthus [9].
A French-language report describes a transnasal canthopexy technique [10]; an aesthetic lateral canthoplasty paper by Taban is also published [15].
A looksmax.org thread announces medial canthus and PFL lengthening surgeries as newly available [3].
A Libyan Journal of Medicine review reports surgical management of eyelid malignancies, including medial canthus reconstruction [8].
looksmax.org threads on inner-corner tattooing and cutting circulate, with posters citing TikTok creators [2][5][6].
Clinics in Plastic Surgery publishes a review of applied lower-eyelid anatomy [4].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the inner eye corner is discussed in threads about tattoos, cutting and surgery, with before and after photos and frequent disagreement [2][5].

claims.claim: A subtle inner-corner tattoo can create the illusion of a lower inner and higher outer eye corner.
claims.believers: One poster relays a creator who reported fixing "droppy eyes" and says the after image looks better and the effect is subtle enough to be read subconsciously [2].
claims.experts: No published study has evaluated cosmetic tattooing at the inner eye corner.

claims.claim: Cutting the medial canthus gives a more striking eye area.
claims.believers: Some posters ask whether the cut is worth it for a more striking eye area [6] and the practice is promoted on TikTok per another thread [5].
claims.experts: Canthal surgery appears in the medical literature as reconstruction or canthopexy by surgeons [8][10]; no study evaluates self-performed cutting. Forum replies themselves cite infection and scarring risk [5][6].

claims.claim: Eye-area appeal depends on the inner corner as well as outer-corner tilt.
claims.believers: Posters ask how to get a "better medial canthus" and compare inner and outer corners in photos as part of eye-area analysis [5][6].
claims.experts: Surgeons quoted in beauty media say tilt is not a primary factor in consultation and that overall facial balance matters more [11]. No published study isolates the inner corner in attractiveness ratings.

claims.claim: Medial canthus surgery is now available and lengthens the eye.
claims.believers: A 2021 thread title presents medial canthus and PFL lengthening surgeries as "finally here" [3].
claims.experts: Canthoplasty is described in reference sources as surgery on the inner and/or outer corner used for cosmetic and functional purposes [15]; epicanthoplasty is described as demanding because of the tear-drainage canals, with scarring the main complication [14].
